entry.title: I Built a Design Skill to Make AI-Generated Websites Less Generic — FireBall v3
entry.summary:
I Built a Design Skill to Make AI-Generated Websites Less Generic — FireBall v3
AI can generate a website in seconds. But there's a problem: a lot of AI-generated websites end up looking the same. The same rounded cards. I wanted to change that. FireBall is an open-source design skill designed to help AI coding and design agents create interfaces that feel more intentional and adapted to the project. Instead of forcing every project into the same visual style, FireBall focuses on understanding the context of the design and giving the AI more freedom to make appropriate decisions. v3 is now available. The main improvements are: Denser designs — more information and stronger layouts without automatically making the interface messy. More design freedom — fewer rigid constraints and more room for the AI to adapt. Better adaptation — the design can better reflect the product, its purpose, and its visual direction. The goal isn't to make every AI-generated website look different just for the sake of being different. The goal is to make the design feel like it was actually designed for the project. Two upcoming versions are officially planned: A dedicated version focused on Image-to-Website, with a complete system specifically designed for turning visual references into websites. More freedom in the design process, giving the AI even more room to make creative decisions. There are also ideas for a v4, including a larger restructuring of the skill, overall improvements, and better generated designs. However, v4 is not officially announced yet. FireBall is open source, and you can check out the project here: https://github.com/Lerat-tlmnul/Fireball-DesignSkill I'd love to hear feedback from developers and designers. Does giving AI more design freedom actually produce better interfaces? What would you change? I'm still working on FireBall, and v3 is only the beginning. 🔥

entry.summary: A year ago, connecting a model to your tools meant writing glue for that model, in that framework, with that vendor's function-calling format. Swap the model and you rewrote the glue. In 2026, that pain is mostly gone, and the reason has a boring name: the Model Context Protocol (MCP). MCP is worth understanding not because it's clever, but because it's winning — and the reason it's winning tells you where the industry's center of gravity is moving. Strip away the branding and MCP is a small client–server contract for connecting language models to the outside world.
